name: Shor
confidence_why: Chispiyakov 1992, Babushkin and Donidze 1966 with Donidze 1996 (as summarised by Kazagasheva 2016) and Dyrenkova 1941 (as summarised by Selyutina 2022) all put Shor stress on the final syllable by default, and differ only in how they treat the root-internal exceptions in which an open or long vowel draws the stress onto an earlier syllable (köbür 'coal', saasqan 'magpie'), Chispiyakov adding that the stressed syllable is often hard to hear because of unreduced unstressed vowels and unwritten half-length.
catalog_citation: Чиспияков, Э. Ф. 1992. Учебник шорского языка: Пособие для преподавателей и студентов. Кемерово: Кемеровское книжное издательство. 318 с. ISBN 5-7550-0338-6.
catalog_locator: Урок Д, §II «Ударение», pp. 35-36 of (archive.org item); pages rendered to PNG and read
catalog_quote: Принято считать, что ударение в двух-, трех- и более сложных словах в шорском языке падает на последний слог. Однако безударное полногласие (см. урок В) не всегда позволяет четко определить, какой слог можно считать ударным, а какой безударным. Затрудняет определение ударения также долгота (точнее, полудолгота) гласных, не отмечаемая в орфографии. Для русского уха полудолгота и полногласие часто могут восприниматься как ударение, что не всегда верно. [...] Ударение может падать на некоторые аффиксы, независимо от их положения в слове (например, аффиксы отрицания -па, -ба, -ма): полбадым «я не был», кӧрбедим «я не видел», қонмадыбыс «мы не ночевали», паспады «он не писал».

new_statements.translation: It is generally held that in Shor, stress in words of two, three or more syllables falls on the last syllable. However, unstressed full vowels (see Lesson В) do not always allow one to determine clearly which syllable should be counted as stressed and which as unstressed. Determination of stress is also made difficult by vowel length (more precisely, half-length), which is not marked in the orthography. [...] Stress may fall on certain affixes irrespective of their position in the word (for example the negative affixes -па, -ба, -ма): полбадым 'I was not', кӧрбедим 'I did not see', конмадыбыс 'we did not spend the night', паспады 'he did not write'.

The quoted sentences are there word for word: 'Принято считать, что ударение в двух-, трех- и более сложных словах в шорском языке падает на последний слог. Однако безударное полногласие (с…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable of the (polysyllabic) word, with two qualifications: the negative suffixes -па/-ба/-ма attract stress wherever they stand, and stress is contrastive for -та/-да (stressed = locative case affix, unstressed = clitic particle). The author warns that unreduced unstressed vowels and unmarked half-length make the stressed syllable hard to hear for Russian ears. Selyutina 2022 (p. 259) reports Dyrenkova 1941 as saying the same: last-syllable, quantitative stress, with exceptions on the first syllable / a syllable with a wide vowel (парбаадым, келбеессин).
new_statements.exceptions: Negative affixes -па/-ба/-ма take stress regardless of position; stressed vs unstressed -та/-да distinguishes locative affix from particle; recent loanwords keep the stress of the source language (p. 36). Dyrenkova (per Selyutina 2022) notes exceptions where stress falls on the first syllable or on a syllable with a wide vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (двух-, трех- и более сложные слова); citation forms and inflected verb forms. The textbook describes the literary language, said to be based on the speech of the Shors of Myski (p. 212 of scanned text), and follows the Kondoma variant of affix pronunciation (footnote 7, p. 25).
new_statements.identity_note: shor1247 is the language-level Shor code. Chispiyakov 1992 describes the literary Shor language, which he says was based on the speech of the Shors of the town of Myski (lower Mrassu/Tom area) and which, for affix vowel harmony, he presents in the Kondoma pronunciation variant (footnote 7, p. 25: 'Здесь и далее мы будем придерживаться кондомского варианта произношения'). Dyrenkova 1941 (reported via Selyutina 2022) is based on the Mrassu dialect.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Shor is usually on the last syllable, as shown in examples (68) a-c: (68) a. mɐl'tʌ 'ax' b. qɯmïs'qa 'ant' c. tyl'gy 'fox' (f.) (Babushkin & Donidze, 1996, p. 468). However, there are multiple exceptions to that when, for example, the stress falls on the first syllable; e.g., in the disyllabic words with close vowels in the second syllable the stress falls on the first syllable, as in (69) a-c: (69) a. 'købʏr 'coal', 'charcoal' b. 't͜ʃʌdïʁ 'life' c. 'qɒnʊq 'life', 'household' [...] Secondary stress occurs in polysyllabic words. When the word lengthens in the process of suffixation, the primary stress moves to the final syllable of the word, while the secondary stress falls on the first syllable [...] unless the final suffix is the unstressed suffix

When the word lengthens in the process of suffixation, the primary stress moves to the final syllable of the word, while the secondary stress falls on the first syllable, as in (69) above—unless t…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final stress, final stress) and as the existing Chispiyakov 1992 statement ('ударение.. падает на последний слог'); adds detail the catalog lacks: initial secondary stress in long suffixed words, a class of unstressed suffixes, and the root-internal open-over-close and long-over-short overrides that put stress on a non-final syllable in words like 'købyr, 'sɑ:sqɑn. All of this is relayed from Babushkin & Donidze 1996 (p. 468) and Donidze 1996 (p. 499), not from the author's own fieldwork.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is normally on the last syllable of the word, and it moves onto the final suffix as suffixes are added (mɐl'tʌ + pɯs → mɐltʌ'bɯs 'our ax'), unless that suffix belongs to the class of unstressed suffixes. Within the root, the thesis (relaying Donidze 1996, p. 499) gives a quality/quantity conditioning: in bases whose short vowels are of the same backness the stress is final; where an open (broad) vowel and a close (narrow) vowel co-occur the stress goes to the open vowel whatever its position (qɯmïs'qɑ, qɒ'nʊq, 'købyr); where a long and a short vowel co-occur it goes to the long vowel (qɑ'rɑ:, 'sɑ:sqɑn). Loanwords keep the stress of the source language (Russian).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'Secondary stress occurs in polysyllabic words. When the word lengthens in the process of suffixation, the primary stress moves to the final syllable of the word, while the secondary stress falls on the first syllable' (p. 109), example ˌpɐrt͜ʃïtqɑnnʌrɢ'ɑ 'to the coming ones' (Dat.), credited to Donidze 1996, p. 499.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Disyllables with a close vowel in the second syllable are stressed on the first syllable ('købʏr 'charcoal', 't͜ʃʌdïʁ 'life', 'qɒnʊq 'household'); more generally stress goes to an open vowel over a close one and to a long vowel over a short one regardless of position. (b) A set of unstressed suffixes never take the stress; the negation -pa/-ba, plural -lɛr/-lʌr and locative -ta/-da are named as stressed suffixes (par´badɯm, qaraq´ta, it͜ʃɛ'lɛrgɛ). (c) 'Stress in borrowed words typically remains the same as in the language that it was borrowed from' (p. 110). (d) p. 12 (dialect survey): the Upper Mrassu subdialect is said to have 'a special kind of stress and intonation', not described further.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Shor generally, drawing its stress data from Babushkin & Donidze 1996 and Donidze 1996; it states that the Shor literary language is based on the Mrassu dialect (pp. 11-12, 156). It notes without detail that the Upper Mrassu subdialect has 'a special kind of stress and intonation' (p. 12). The author is of Shor heritage (dedication) but the stress section is a literature summary, not original instrumental work.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: the catalog (final), Chispiyakov 1992 (final, with the caveat that unstressed full vowels and vowel length make the stressed syllable hard to hear) and Kazagasheva 2016 (final 'usually') agree. The only tension is one of degree: Kazagasheva, following Donidze, lists systematic non-final cases (open vowel attracts stress over a close one, long vowel over a short one, e.g. 'købyr, 'sɑ:sqɑn) which make the system partly quality/weight-sensitive within roots, while the catalog rule string encodes pure final stress. Since the default and the outcome under suffixation are final, the catalog reading stands; the overrides are best recorded as exceptions/refinement rather than as a change of type.
